shows.title: Nuria Maria: Blues Rouge
shows.description:
Blues Rouge is Nuria Maria's second solo show at Cadogan's Milan space, following 2024's Tule Tänne | Come Here. The Netherlands-based painter works in a loose, atmospheric abstraction — still lifes, stretched-out landscapes and architectural fragments rendered somewhere between recognizable and dissolved, built from fields of acrylic blues, plums and reds on linen and canvas.

Maria's project has always been about mood over description: a certain quality of light in a window, the temperature of a room, a half-remembered walk. Blues Rouge leans into a set of contrasts she's been circling for a few years now — warm color against cool shade, old stone against new construction, noise against quiet — treating a painting less as a picture of something and more as a register of a feeling that happened once, on a particular kind of day.

Works range from small drawings and still lifes to large-scale diptychs, giving a sense of how she moves between intimate and expansive registers using the same loose, atmospheric vocabulary. Worth seeing for anyone drawn to the current strain of European lyrical abstraction that treats color as narrative material rather than decoration.

shows.title: La generazione felice (The Happy Generation)
shows.dates_note: Venue's exhibitions page gives only "Until 3 October" for the closing date; no opening date is published.
shows.description:
Nazar Strelyaev-Nazarko paints in the deliberate, layered manner of old-master portraiture, then aims that technique at deeply unglamorous subjects: hanging socks, improvised forts made of couch cushions, a woman riding an ostrich in a turban. The tension between the gravity of the medium and the silliness of the scene is the whole point — history painting turned toward the ordinary and the absurd.

The strongest works here are a triptych following a child's blanket fort from construction to collapse, and a pair of large "portraits" of figures dressed in clothes that clearly aren't theirs, play-acting at adulthood. Throughout, faces carry the same heavy-lidded, half-asleep expression, and compositions leave a deliberate crack in the illusion — a doorway, a sliver of real sky — so the constructed nature of each scene never fully disappears.

Strelyaev-Nazarko, born in Kharkiv in 1998 and now based in Milan, filters a childhood shaped by the ambient anxieties of post-Soviet Ukraine through the vocabulary of European painting he studied at Brera and NABA. This is his second solo show with Ncontemporary, following Butterfly Hunt at the gallery's Venice space, and it's a good entry point to an artist whose work has quietly circulated from Marsèll Paradise to a Louis Vuitton runway. Worth seeing for the painting technique alone, but the melancholy underneath the playfulness is what stays with you.

shows.title: The Skin of Time
shows.description:
Felix Schramm's third solo outing at RIBOT continues his long-running argument that sculpture is really a question of what happens when architecture stops behaving. On the ground floor, three large plasterboard-and-silver-leaf panels from the ongoing Dark Site series let a decade of slow oxidation do the composing: debris and studio detritus are sealed under silver leaf and left to tarnish, so the image keeps changing long after the piece leaves the studio. Mirrored inserts cut into the panels pull the room itself into the work, blurring where the sculpture ends and the gallery begins.

A new floor-to-ceiling sculpture from the Accumulation series — a crumpled sheet of copper hanging from a strap above an emptied-out plexiglass pedestal — pushes the same idea toward something closer to still life, with the pedestal's usual job (holding up an object) replaced by its opposite (housing a fragment, doing nothing structural at all). Downstairs, new 2026 Dark Site pieces introduce a jolt of red plexiglass, and an Intersection installation — the body of work that first put Schramm on Milan's map in 2015 — tears into the architecture of the room directly, the same aggressive, wall-breaking gesture that opened RIBOT eleven years ago.

Schramm (b. 1970, Hamburg; based in Düsseldorf) has now had three exhibitions here since RIBOT's opening, and it's a program his practice fits unusually well: a small two-floor space that gets structurally reconsidered with every show he does in it. The special-project edition of ten A4-scale Dark Site works, made for this occasion, is a good way to see his material process at a scale you can hold in your head all at once.

shows.title: True Reality
shows.description:
Benjamin Jones's first institutional show in Italy brings together new and previously exhibited work built from an ongoing investigation into natural history museums and botanical gardens across Europe — the very apparatus of conservation, classification and display that turns living nature into "specimens" and "knowledge." Working mainly through photography, Jones is interested in the moment a piece of the natural world gets pulled out of context and re-staged inside an institutional system of vitrines, labels and taxonomies.

The London-based, Reading-born artist treats the museum diorama and the herbarium drawer as subjects in their own right, examining how supposedly neutral scientific display is really a highly constructed form of storytelling. The show's title plays on that tension: what counts as "true" once nature has been curated, lit, and captioned for an audience.

The exhibition also folds in two new contributions by Linda Fregni Nagler and Stefano Graziani, both printed for the first time on this occasion, extending Jones's inquiry into photography's role in constructing versions of reality into a wider conversation with artists working similarly at the edges of documentary and fiction. It's a smart entry point for Fondazione Elpis's Villa space, since the theme — the manufacture of "truth" through systems of display — resonates with the foundation's own role in staging and framing younger artists' work.

shows.title: L'idea del colore
shows.description:
ABC-ARTE's Milan space follows its Genoa presentation of Jorrit Tornquist with a second, independently conceived chapter devoted to the Austrian-Italian colorist, developed with the Jorrit Tornquist Archive. Tornquist spent more than sixty years treating color not as a property applied to form but as the raw material of vision itself, and this show pulls together paintings and works on paper from the 1960s through the 2010s to trace that single, sustained inquiry.

The centerpiece is XY diagonale (2013), a large enamel-on-aluminum floor piece on a steel base that grew out of a 1975 project: rather than sitting on a wall, the color becomes an object you walk around, turning the act of looking into something physical. Around it hang smaller acrylic and mixed-media canvases spanning decades, letting visitors see how Tornquist's palette and geometric vocabulary shifted while his core question — what color does to our perception of space — stayed constant.

Tornquist worked at the intersection of art, architecture and color theory, and this compact survey is a good entry point for anyone curious about the more scientific, perceptual wing of postwar Italian abstraction, alongside contemporaries like Getulio Alviani or Bruno Munari.

shows.title: XYZ
shows.description:
Aki Sasamoto's first institutional show in Europe brings together two decades of work that sits somewhere between sculpture, performance, dance and stand-up comedy. Trained in mathematics before switching to dance and then visual art, Sasamoto builds installations that double as stage sets: everyday objects — laundry machines, kitchen tools, bar furniture — get rigged into kinetic contraptions that she or invited performers activate live, turning the gallery into a lab for watching how bodies, habits and social norms collide.

The title "XYZ" is doing several jobs at once: the last three letters of the alphabet, the coordinates of three-dimensional space, the variables physicists use to describe where a particle probably is, and — per its use as American slang — a discreet heads-up that your zipper is undone. That mix of the cosmic and the mundane is the whole point. Sasamoto has said her work grows out of an outsider's attention to the small absurdities of daily life, filtered through the discipline of geometry and the loose logic of improvisation she picked up from John Cage and Alvin Lucier.

Expect a mix of sculptural installations, video documentation of past performances (including pieces first staged at SculptureCenter, Para Site Hong Kong and the Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo), and new work made for the Shed, HangarBicocca's space reserved for younger and mid-career artists. It's a strange, funny, occasionally unsettling introduction to an artist who has spent twenty years turning ordinary gestures into choreography.

shows.title: Abitare lo spazio (Inhabiting Space)
shows.description:
Nearly twenty years after his death, Luciano Fabro gets Italy's first museum retrospective devoted to his work, and HangarBicocca's cavernous Navate — the same space that has hosted Anselm Kiefer's permanent Seven Heavenly Palaces — is the right scale for it. Around fifty sculptures and installations trace Fabro's career from the mirrored, reflective pieces of the 1960s through to the later "habitats," full architectural environments built from paper and light that he saw less as objects to look at than as spaces to be lived in.

Fabro was a central, if characteristically independent, figure in Arte Povera, and the show leans into the idea that anchors his whole practice: habitat, a word he adopted only in the 1980s but was working toward from the start, fusing the Latin habito (to dwell) with habitus (bearing, form, dress). Marble, bronze, glass, lead and silk all show up, each chosen for a specific sensory quality rather than any fixed hierarchy of "serious" versus "humble" materials — a very Arte Povera refusal that Fabro pushed further than most of his peers into genuinely inhabitable structures.

The retrospective, curated by Fiammetta Griccioli, Roberta Tenconi and Vicente Todolí with Fabro's own archive, also doubles as a homecoming: Fabro moved to Milan in 1959 and taught at the Brera Academy from 1983 to 2002, shaping a generation of Milanese artists. Seeing his mirrored cubes, silk-and-glass pieces and paper habitats reassembled at this scale, decades after they were made, is a rare chance to test how radical his ideas about sculpture and the body still feel.

shows.title: Immagini del vuoto: dalla camera oscura alla camera chiara
shows.description:
This is the first show Vistamare has mounted since the death of Mimmo Jodice (Naples, 1933–2025), one of the defining figures of postwar Italian photography, and the gallery's fourth exhibition of his work overall. Rather than a straightforward retrospective, it's conceived as a three-part dialogue: curator Andrea Viliani has invited two artists deeply engaged with the history and material conditions of photography, Linda Fregni Nagler and Armin Linke, to work alongside material drawn from the Jodice archive, including some pieces never shown before.

Jodice spent decades treating the camera not as a tool for recording the world but as an instrument for thinking about it — his black-and-white images of Naples, the Mediterranean, and classical statuary are less documents than meditations on presence and absence. The show's title, translating roughly as "images of the void," points to that undercurrent in his work: a preoccupation with emptiness, stillness, and the gap between what a photograph captures and what a photograph is. An unsent letter by Jodice, addressed to an imagined interlocutor, is reportedly installed at the center of the exhibition as a kind of thesis statement for the whole project.

Expect a mix of vintage prints and archival ephemera — proofs, contact sheets, and other traces of Jodice's working process — arranged across the gallery's rooms with attention to how natural light changes through the space, itself a nod to Jodice's own obsession with the physics of the photographic image. For anyone who knows Jodice mainly through his best-known Mediterranean and Napoli series, this is a chance to see the more private, process-oriented side of his archive, framed by two contemporary artists whose own work has long been in conversation with his.

shows.title: Piante Vagabonde
shows.description:
Clarissa Tossin's Piante Vagabonde ("Vagabond Plants") takes its title from the weeds that colonize sidewalk cracks, roadsides and vacant lots — species written off as invasive but resilient enough to root themselves almost anywhere. The Brazilian artist, whose work has long probed the entanglement of colonial history, ecology and the body, makes these plants literal collaborators: canvases are printed by pressing actual foraged specimens directly onto the surface using block-printing ink, so that leaf, stem and root leave their own trace alongside the imprint of the artist's body.

The resulting large-format works read as hybrid botanical rubbings and figure studies at once — ghostly silhouettes of burdock, wild strawberry, cinquefoil and sticky weed overlapping with the pressure of a hand or torso. It's a quiet but pointed argument against the idea that humans stand outside the ecosystems they disturb: the same margins and disturbed soils that let these "vagabond" plants take hold are the ones shaped by histories of extraction and displacement that Tossin's broader practice keeps returning to.

This Milan presentation follows directly from her recent museum survey Point of No Return at MASP in São Paulo, and brings a European debut of works first developed in Rome and Los Angeles — a chance to see, up close, how differently the same working method reads depending on which city's weeds end up on the canvas.

shows.title: Tenki Hiramatsu
shows.description:
Tenki Hiramatsu, a Japanese-born painter who trained in Tokyo before settling in Karlsruhe, Germany, paints noirish, faintly cartoonish characters that drift through loosely resolved, atmospheric grounds. His figures — recurring types in top hats, boxers, solitary men mid-gesture — carry the outward look of narrative painting without ever settling into an actual story; Hiramatsu works intuitively and without preliminary sketches, letting each canvas find its own logic as he goes.

The effect, across a body of work built up over the past decade in shows in London, Zurich and Los Angeles, is of images that seem to warp slightly the longer you look at them, characters who feel glimpsed rather than fully described. This exhibition, opening alongside Clarissa Tossin's Piante Vagabonde in the gallery's other rooms, marks Hiramatsu's first solo outing in Milan and a chance to see how his particular strain of hazy, deadpan figuration reads outside the German and Anglo-American contexts where he has mostly shown to date.

shows.title: Controcorrente
shows.description:
Uwe Wittwer's first Italian solo show digs into two colonial-era photographic archives — the Basel Mission's missionary photographs and the ethnographic collection of Oxford's Pitt Rivers Museum — and reworks their images of West and Central Africa, India, southern China and the Americas in watercolor, paint and drawing. The Swiss painter, who has spent decades appropriating and distorting found photographs and art-historical images, treats the archive not as neutral documentation but as evidence of the point of view and power structures that produced it in the first place; his overpainting, blurring and reframing of these pictures is a way of interrogating what got left out of the historical record.

The exhibition's title, meaning "against the current" or "upstream," refers to the river routes — the Congo, the Amazon, the great waterways of Asia — that colonial expeditions once used to push into continents' interiors, and doubles as a description of the show's own method of tracing images back toward their point of origin. A separate strand pairs two Milan-held Old Master paintings, Caravaggio's Basket of Fruit and Veronese's Last Supper, with a group of watercolors after the ship draughtsman Willem van de Velde, linking seventeenth-century Dutch maritime power to the same colonial currents running through the photographic material.

It's a show built on hard, specific research rather than easy gestures, and one that uses painting's slowness — the time it takes to rework an image by hand — as a way of holding uncomfortable material still long enough to actually look at it.

shows.title: VINCVLVM
shows.description:
Cveto Maršič, a Slovenian painter formed in the informalist tradition, builds his canvases out of earth-toned, heavily worked surfaces that read less as landscape depictions than as material records of a physical relationship with land itself — the ground he was born on, the ground he now lives and works on, and the rhythms of viticulture and seasonal labor that shape both. VINCVLVM, Latin for "bond" or "link," names the show's underlying idea: that place, memory, gesture and even music accumulate in layers on the canvas the way sediment accumulates in soil.

Maršič builds his paintings through repeated overpainting, so that earlier marks, words and traces are never fully erased — they surface again through later layers like things time couldn't quite bury. The landscapes that emerge aren't pictures to be read at a glance but residues of bodily, repeated contact with a place, closer to a record of experience than a view.

Coming from an artist trained at the Ljubljana Academy whose work sits in public collections from Palma de Mallorca to Valencia, this is a chance to see a painter still mining a decades-old vein of land-based abstraction with evident conviction.
